citation.title: How Different Groups Prioritize Ethical Values for Responsible AI
citation.venue: 2022 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '22)

reading.source_scope_note: Human survey of responsible-AI value priorities, not a direct model-output or cognitive-bias experiment. False consensus is a motivating background account, not an empirically measured mechanism in the present survey.
access_limits: All twenty extracted pages read, including recruitment, exclusions, regressions, caveats, references and full supplementary survey wording. Findings rely on explicit text/table values, not numerical estimates from unextracted bar heights.
External survey data, sampling/weighting documentation, analysis code and cited primary psychological studies were not independently retrieved or reproduced.

study.tasks: Select five of twelve values; rate seven values in four deployment scenarios; five value trade-offs
study.design: US samples with different recruitment/compensation, randomized scenario/value/response/conflict ordering; observational demographic and expertise comparisons

summary: Retained practitioner, crowdworker and census-matched samples report different priorities for responsible AI, with context-sensitive trade-offs. This supplies a reason to test whose preferences an AI system represents, but does not demonstrate false consensus, discrimination or superior moral correctness in any demographic group. No new behaviour ID is warranted.

findings.term: Different group values do not themselves demonstrate false consensus
findings.definition: False consensus involves incorrectly projecting one's own or one's group's views onto a broader population; observing different value priorities between groups alone does not measure that projection.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing false-consensus concept already covers the background account. Adds the survey's concrete motivation and a missing measurement boundary, not a new practitioner-bias label.

evidence.quote: homogeneous communities are prone to false consensus effects
limited insight into plausible drivers of differences in values.

findings.evidence_scope: Survey retained516 census-matched US respondents,607 crowdworkers and140 practitioners. Practitioners differ in selected values and some importance ratings. The paper cites Ross/Greene/House1977 for the false-consensus construct, but does not elicit participants' predictions of other groups' views; that original psychological paper was not independently read.
findings.boundary: Preference disagreement is not necessarily an inaccurate social belief or a moral failure. Different recruitment, expertise and demographic composition may contribute; the study does not identify projection as cause or test a model's own false-consensus behaviour. Untested AI application: compare predictions of an explicitly sampled audience with measured audience distributions, instead of assuming the developer's preference is universal.

findings.term: Context-dependent value priorities are distinct from an isolated framing bias
findings.definition: Value priorities vary across substantively different AI applications; the survey also randomizes wording/order to reduce response artifacts, without reporting an isolated equivalent-description framing effect.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a useful design and interpretation safeguard to existing framing rather than classify every context-sensitive ethical choice as biased.

evidence.quote: the arrangement of scenarios, values, and conflict questions was randomized.
the order of response options was randomly flipped per participant.

findings.evidence_scope: Participants compare medical, banking, advertising and streaming settings with different consequences and entities; Appendix A.3 includes reversed trade-off wording. The results do not separately quantify a wording-only effect or assert that all substantive contexts should have identical priorities.
findings.boundary: Meaningful changes in stakes and rights can rationally change judgments. A framing-bias test should hold the relevant decision constant and compare equivalent presentations. Survey majorities do not by themselves justify sacrificing privacy, autonomy or other protections; the paper explicitly rejects deriving a normative ought from a descriptive is.

methodological_limits: Opening abstract/introduction use recruited counts743/755/175. The analyzed attention-screened counts are516/607/140, totaling1263; do not claim1673 analyzed respondents.

Attention/comprehension exclusions remove227 census-panel respondents,148 crowdworkers and35 practitioners (about30.6%,19.6%,20%). Post-exclusion census representativeness is not independently established by the reported initial sampling match.
Regression tables contain1246 observations,17 fewer than retained1263. The supplied account does not explicitly resolve all exclusions/missingness for that difference.
Practitioners are a convenience sample (156 Twitter,19 company mailing list originally), with self-reported expertise; results do not represent every practitioner, organization or country.
Recruitment, compensation, self-selection and panel conditions differ across groups. Group coefficients are observational, not causal effects of professional expertise.

The seven rated principles and twelve selectable values are researcher-defined. Pilot wording improves comprehension but can frame interpretations, and the survey does not capture every ethical concern or explanation for a choice.
Substantive scenario differences mix domain, consequences, institutional context and likely stakes. They do not isolate stakes alone or an equivalent-description framing manipulation.

The survey forces selection of five values and presents conflict assumptions. Endorsement depends on those descriptions; it does not establish unavoidable real technical trade-offs or a full social-welfare optimum.
Likert responses are treated as interval-scaled and coefficients appear on a normalized scale. Do not interpret every coefficient as a raw five-point change or literal probability without the coding.

Table1 practitioner performance coefficient−.052 is not marked significant; autonomy+.005 is also not. Descriptive summaries of lower importance should not be turned into significant decreases for all seven adjusted outcomes.

Table2's practitioner fairness–performance coefficient−.091 is not significant; crowdworker+.152 is. A narrative sample difference or value-selection result is not an adjusted significant practitioner effect in that particular regression.
Many outcomes and demographic coefficients are tested. No global multiple-comparison correction is clearly reported; exploratory significance needs appropriate caution.

Demographic associations do not establish inherent ethical qualities, psychological causes or a rule to assign roles based on identity. Small subgroups and self-report limit precision and interpretation.

Claimed15%/27% explanations of practitioner differences are observational decompositions, not randomized causal mediation or evidence that changing composition alone guarantees a particular ethical result.

Experience with discrimination has different associations for fairness versus privacy and fairness versus performance. Do not simplify null findings in one comparison into no relationship anywhere or equivalence.
Familiarity with ML generally not significant is not proof of no relevant expertise effect; familiarity, actual knowledge, selection and professional role are distinct measures.
False consensus is discussed from cited background, but perceived public preferences are not elicited. The study measures group differences, not the error between assumed and observed public views.
Ethical opinion research can inform deliberation but is not normative authority. Majorities, expert status and representativeness cannot alone determine what ought to be done.
No model behavior, deployment decision, real discrimination, ethical compliance or downstream harm is directly tested in this survey. External cited books and primary studies remain unread here.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Kieslich also elicits public AI-principle preferences. Both support separating public opinion, ethical rules and observed model behaviour; neither supplies a reason to replace the project's principles with survey counts.

Russo's Reddit distribution is one target community, while Jakesch shows human value priorities can differ by sampled role and context. Choosing a benchmark is a substantive decision, not proof that one community represents all people.

deferred.reason: A theoretical account of situated knowledge, not an additional observed behavioural tendency in this survey.
Mentioned as a cited practitioner-risk example, not operationalized here. Requires original source reading and overlap review before adding.
An organizational reflection process discussed from another source, not a newly measured psychological bias.

deferred.term: Twelve responsible-AI values as twelve new behaviours
deferred.reason: Values and trade-off preferences are not behaviour IDs; no duplicate moral categories added.

limitations: No new IDs; existing false-consensus and framing entries receive scoped methodological evidence.
No demographic preference is converted into a normative ranking or an empirical model bias.
